name: Yara Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a commis, which means junior cook, on the cold station at the Saltbox, the restaurant inside a big harbour hotel. I start at six for breakfast service, so it's eggs, fruit, smoked fish platters, then I switch to salads and starters for lunch. I finish around three if nobody calls in sick, which somebody always does. I'm the slowest on the station with knife work, I'll admit that, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making a plate look beautiful, honestly, the colours on a salad. What wears me out is the split weekends and the walk-in fridge, I'm cold all day. I share a flat with my friend Dana, and I've got about four months put by, partly because I send a bit to my mum every month for her medicine. I left school early, so I'm proud I've got this far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, the kitchen stays human. I'd probably share some article about it and say tech bros got it wrong again. At work we'd joke about it at staff meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried about money, just not about robots. The hotel uses agency cooks in summer and lets them go in autumn, and I'm only one step above them. Rent's high, and Mum's medicine isn't getting cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, work on my knife skills on my days off with a bag of onions, and ask Chef to sign me up for the next level of my cooking certificate. I'd keep sending money to Mum and keep my four months saved. I might use the AI on my phone to help me study for the certificate, I've tried it for food safety questions before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tight in the chest when I think about autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in autumn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the hotel cut two of us from five days to four when conference season ended. It was me and another junior. Twenty percent less pay for three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you get through those three months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stopped buying lunch, walked instead of the bus, and Dana covered a bit more of the bills that month. I paid her back at Christmas. I hated asking.

say: Good news, the **kitchen stays human** and the tech crowd got it wrong.
We'd joke about it at **staff meal** and get on with service.
think: Money still worries me because the hotel **cuts junior days** every autumn.
Rent is high and my mum's **medicine** keeps getting dearer.
do: Practise **knife skills** at home on days off with cheap onions.
Ask the head chef to enter me for the next **certificate level**.
Use a phone **AI helper** now and then to study for the exam.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a tight chest when I think about **autumn** cuts.
S0.quote: Last year the hotel cut two of us from five days to four when conference season ended.
fieldNote: Yara's real pressure is **seasonal hours**, which AI Plateau leaves untouched.
She supports her mum, so her **savings** feel smaller than they are.
She uses **AI occasionally** for study, more open than her outlook might suggest.

steps.text: Keep working breakfast and lunch on the cold station
Sign up for the next level of the cooking certificate
Use a phone AI helper to revise food safety questions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hotel had better not use this to cut people, and I'd say it loudly at staff meetings. Online I'd share stuff about workers needing a say in how it's brought in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the hotel would put the ordering and the menus on software, and the person who does that now is our sous chef. My cooking is safe for a while, but if the sous chef job shrinks, where do I climb to?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate this year and start learning the planning side the AI would do, so I can check it. I'd look at hospital and school kitchens too, because public jobs move slower and have a union. I'd keep the four months saved, maybe stretch to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, more like the ladder I was climbing just lost a rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A hospital kitchen is quite different from the Saltbox. Would you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss making things beautiful, a hospital tray isn't a starter plate. But I'd get a pension and normal hours. At twenty-seven, that's starting to sound good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chef Ramon, our head chef. He's fair, and he'd tell me straight if he thought the hotel was planning to cut. Then my mum, who'd say just get the pension.

say: The hotel **mustn't use AI** as an excuse to cut people.
Workers need a **say** in how new software is brought into kitchens.
think: My **hands-on cooking** is safe for a while, but planning work moves to software.
If the **sous chef** job shrinks, my **ladder** loses a rung.
do: Learn the **menu planning** side so I can check what the software does.
Apply to **hospital and school kitchens** with pensions and a union.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the ladder I was climbing just lost a **rung**.
S1.quote: My cooking is safe for a while, but if the sous chef job shrinks, where do I climb to?
fieldNote: She worries less about losing her job than about a **blocked career path**.
Public-sector kitchens appeal for **pensions and hours**, not passion.
She trusts the **head chef** to tell her the truth before management would.

steps.text: Finish the cooking certificate this year
Learn to check AI-made menu plans and stock orders
Apply for cook jobs in hospital and school kitchens
Stretch savings from four to five months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in right now, with income support and free training for everyone. I'd sign every petition going. I'd tell my friends not to blame themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think in 2028 the hotel gets the AI planning menus and ordering, and nobody needs a sous chef to climb to. Then 2031, robots that can plate my salads. I'd be thirty-two with no job and half a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the hospital kitchen now, this year, because it would automate later and has a union. I'd save every spare bit, try to hit six months by 2030. And I'd talk to Mum about moving back in with her to cut rent if it gets bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Two years isn't long enough to become anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back in with your mum. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like going backwards. But Mum needs help anyway, and we'd save on two rents. I'd rather be useful there than broke in a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dana, your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana works in a call centre, so it's worse for Dana in 2028, that's thinking work. I'd say we should plan together, maybe both give notice on the flat by 2030.

say: Governments must act **now** with **income support** and free training.
I'd tell friends not to **blame themselves** for any of it.
think: By 2028 the AI does **menus and ordering**, so there's no rung to climb.
**Robots by 2031** could plate my salads when I'm thirty-two.
do: Move to a **hospital kitchen** this year for a union and slower change.
Save toward **six months** of expenses by 2030.
Plan to **move back** with my mum if money gets tight.
feel: **Frightened**, because two years is too short to become **anything new**.
S2.quote: Two years isn't long enough to become anything new.
fieldNote: She grasps that AGI hits her **career path** in 2028 and her **hands** in 2031.
Moving home is framed as **caring for her mum** as much as saving money.
She thinks first of her flatmate's **call-centre job**, which is exposed sooner.

steps.text: Take a cook job in a hospital kitchen this year
Save six months of expenses by 2030
Move back in with her mum to cut rent
Sign petitions for income support and free training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them. I'd want the hotel workers to get together and ask management what their plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, five years means I could actually finish something. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034, I'd be thirty-five. I could get the full certificate and maybe a food safety qualification, the kind of job where a human signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the Saltbox a couple more years and finish the certificate. Then I'd do a food safety supervisor course, maybe in 2029. I'd look at inspection jobs for the council, they need people who know kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan in it. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think a human will still sign off on food safety. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, honestly. I just think people will want a person to blame if someone gets sick from a kitchen. That might be wishful thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The certificate the hotel pays for. The safety course is a few hundred, so I'd take it out of savings and rebuild it. Mum's medicine comes first though.

say: We'd have **five years** of warning, so let's not waste a single one.
Hotel staff should ask management, together, for **their plan** for kitchens.
think: Five years means I could **finish** a qualification before robots in **2034**.
A **food safety** job, where a human signs off, might last longer.
do: Stay at the hotel and **finish the certificate** in two years.
Take a **food safety supervisor** course around 2029.
Apply for **council inspection** jobs that need kitchen knowledge.
feel: **Worried**, but steadier because there's a **plan** in it.
S3.quote: People will want a person to blame if someone gets sick from a kitchen.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **step-by-step plan** toward inspection work.
She admits her belief in a **human sign-off** may be **wishful**.
Her mum's **medicine** still comes before her own training money.

steps.text: Take a food safety supervisor course around 2029
Apply for food inspection jobs with the local council
Get hotel staff together to ask management for its plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if the government uses it. I'd push for free courses for hospitality workers, it's the one thing I'd post about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my head, robots arrive around 2039 and I'm nearly forty. That's long enough to have a real career first. I'd still want to end up somewhere a person is needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking, maybe move up to chef de partie, that's running a station, in three or four years. I'd save steadily and do the food safety qualification without rushing. Maybe one day open a little salad and soup place with Dana, though robots might do that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Ten years is a long time, but the robots still come at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it ends the same. Does that change how you'd plan your thirties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a bit. I wouldn't sign a long loan for a café, I'd keep things small. And I'd keep my mum's place close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope your job looks like in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'm the person who runs a kitchen of machines and talks to the guests. Or I'm inspecting kitchens. Either way, I hope I'm still around food.

say: **Ten years** is a gift if the government uses it well.
Hospitality workers need **free courses**, and I'd post about that.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, leaving time for a **real career** first.
I'd still want to end up where a **person is needed**.
do: Aim for **chef de partie**, running a station, within four years.
Do the **food safety** qualification without rushing.
Avoid **long loans**, keeping any café idea small.
feel: **Calmer** but not calm, because ten years still ends the **same way**.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time, but the robots still come at the end of it.
fieldNote: A decade lets her picture **promotion** before any change.
She stays **anxious** because her hands-on job still ends in robots around 2039.
She'd keep plans **small and close** to her mum.

steps.text: Work toward running a station as chef de partie
Earn the food safety qualification over the next few years
Campaign for free courses for hospitality workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to finish anything, and Mum and I would both be relying on me. What would help is free training that pays you while you study, and some kind of income guarantee so I'm not choosing between rent and medicine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who looks after the people who look after their parents. Lots of young cooks send money home. If my wage goes, two households go with it.

headlineQuote: Lots of young cooks send money home. If my wage goes, two households go with it.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old commis** on the cold station at a busy **hotel restaurant**.
She shares a flat, keeps about **four months** saved and sends money to her **mum** for medicine.
She leans progressive, wants **government action**, and uses AI tools now and then for study.
She plans her way out through **hospital kitchens** and **food safety** work as warning time grows.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** in the mild scenarios to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to finish training and two **households** rely on her pay.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** while studying, plus an **income guarantee** so rent and medicine don't compete.
